metadata.title: Attributions & Scholarly Citations
metadata.description: Primary academic and computational sources powering the Urdu Meter Handbook and Interactive Studio.

entries.title: Urdu Meter: A Practical Handbook
entries.urdu_title: اردو بحور: ایک عملی دستی کتاب
entries.publisher_or_affiliation: Department of Middle Eastern, South Asian, and African Studies (MESAAS), Columbia University; South Asian Studies, University of Wisconsin-Madison
entries.summary: The primary intellectual, theoretical, and pedagogical foundation of this software. Pritchett & Khaliq formulated the empirical weight rule ('2 letters = Long (=), 1 letter = Short (-)'), the vertical syllable code-breaking scansion method, the catalog of 37 classical meters grouped into melodic families, the rules of flexibility (x), and the 24 classical ghazal exercises with answer keys.
entries.related_project: Also citing Frances W. Pritchett's monumental online research repository 'A Desertful of Roses: The Divan of Ghalib in Urdu with Complete Scansions and Commentary' (https://franpritchett.com/00ghalib/).

entries.title: Bah'r: The Backbone of Shaayari
entries.urdu_title: بحر: شاعری کی ریڑھ کی ہڈی
entries.summary: A widely-shared plain-language introduction to bah'r, teaching 13 of the most popular bah'rs (each with its arkaan/afa'il and an illustrative sher plus a classic couplet by a named ustaad) via the ghazal community's own ASCII romanization rather than academic transliteration. This app cross-references its 13 named bah'rs against Pritchett's 37-meter catalog (12 of the 13 match cleanly; the 13th, a 4-foot 'Mutadaarik Saalim', is a shortened usage of catalog meter #12 rather than a distinct meter) and folds 11 of its classic couplets in as extra examples on the matching meters in Meter › Lookup. See data/urdupoetry_bahrs.json for the full extraction, meter mapping, and scan verification, and docs/reviews/18-urdupoetry-bahrs.md for the write-up.
entries.related_project: Saved locally at data/sources/urdupoetry_art5.html so the extraction is reproducible.

entries.title: Finite-State AST Graph Transliteration & Multi-Script Parsing Engine (ghalib.js)
entries.urdu_title: محدود المعطیات گراف پر مبنی کثیر الخطی ٹرانسلٹریشن انجن
entries.publisher_or_affiliation: Department of Linguistics, Languages, and Cultures, Michigan State University; Columbia University South Asian Digital Humanities
entries.summary: Developer of the underlying finite-state transition graph and abstract syntax tree parser ('ghalib.js', 'urdu_parser_data.js', 'devanagari_parser_data.js', 'diacritics_parser_data.js') originally installed in October 2002 on Columbia's 'A Desertful of Roses'. In this application, Sean Pue's algorithm powers our multi-script engine, enabling instantaneous switching across Urdu Nastaliq, Devanagari, Roman with academic diacritics, and ASCII.

entries.title: A Desertful of Roses (Ghalib) and A Garden of Kashmir (Mir)
entries.summary: Pritchett's complete Urdu divans of Ghalib and Mir, each verse with its meter, Urdu, Devanagari and Roman. They are the app's Ghalib and Mir collections and the standard the scanner and transliteration are held to: no change may make them scan or read worse.

entries.title: Rekhta
entries.summary: The Urdu poets beyond Ghalib and Mir (Faiz, Jaun Elia and others): Urdu, Devanagari and Roman as Rekhta gives them, each ghazal linked to its Rekhta page. Rekhta names no bahr; the engine reads it from the lines, with the iẓāfat, doubled letters and pen names Rekhta's Roman shows.

entries.title: Urdushahkar
entries.summary: Further Urdu ghazals for the Poets list, linked to their source pages and metered by the engine in the same way.

entries.title: Sufinama
entries.summary: The Persian (Fārsī) ghazals of Hafiz, Rumi, Saadi, ʿIrāqī, Khusrau, Bedil and other Sufi poets, in Urdu script with Sufinama's Roman. The Roman's short vowels and iẓāfat teach the Persian engine (ScanFa) how each word scans.

entries.title: Ganjoor (گنجور)
entries.summary: The reference text of classical Persian poetry, with each poem's meter. Ganjoor's meters fill in the Persian meters of the circles and the Persian-only meters (ids F…); its texts check every Sufinama ghazal's meter and words, and an independent test set of 240 well-known ghazals of Hafiz, Saadi, Rumi and Jami measures how well the Persian scanner reads text it has never seen. Persian ghazals link to their Ganjoor page.

entries.title: The Rhythmic Structure of Persian Poetic Meters
entries.publisher_or_affiliation: PhD dissertation, Department of Linguistics, University of Arizona
entries.summary: The Persian prosody rules the Persian scanner follows where they differ from Urdu: ke, be and the conjunction o may scan long; a syllable holds at most three morae (an overlong syllable is long + short); and two shorts may be sung as one long (muftaʿilun as three longs), as Rumi often does.

entries.title: A Comprehensive Persian-English Dictionary
entries.publisher_or_affiliation: Routledge & K. Paul, London; digital edition: Digital Dictionaries of South Asia (University of Chicago); scraped by Theodore S. Beers (steingass-scraper, MIT)
entries.related_project: steingass-scraper↗ (Theodore S. Beers)
entries.summary: Every headword with its classical pronunciation, short vowels and all. The Persian engine takes from it the syllable weights of some 3,000 words that neither the engine nor Sufinama's Roman reads right.

entries.title: Persian Grammar and Morphology
entries.summary: Reference for where Persian grammar allows an unwritten iẓāfat (not after prepositions, pronouns or verbs, not before a verb or preposition), which the Persian scanner uses to guess the iẓāfat that plain pasted text leaves out.
